experiment.question: At 50 to 100 ms of per-PDU latency, where does Collectd stop completing its collection cycle, and what runs out?
experiment.plan: Inject uniform 50 to 100 ms of delay per packet on the simulator's SNMP interface with netem, representing a real SNMP agent on a chassis that must gather from line cards, hardware planes or the control-plane CPU before it can answer a request. Start at 2,000 devices, measure one 900 s window (three cycles), grow by 500 and repeat, stopping at the first rung that fails the pass criterion. The fleet was held at 3,000. Search upward only: nl6 has no selective delete, so every shrink is a full rebuild.

jvm.flags: JAVA_HEAP_SIZE=10240, JAVA_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE=8192, -XX:+UseG1GC, Prometheus JMX exporter on 9299. Unchanged from the cleanroom run.

sut.config_delta:
Identical to the cleanroom deployment on the OpenNMS side. The only change is on the simulator.

simulator, netsim-benchmark-01
  tc qdisc replace dev enp6s19 root netem delay 75ms 25ms
  uniform 50 to 100 ms per packet on the SNMP interface, responses only
  verified with 200 probes: min 50.6 ms, median 76.0 ms, max 99.8 ms

OpenNMS Core, unchanged from the cleanroom run

  opennms.conf: JAVA_HEAP_SIZE 10240, JAVA_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE 8192, -XX:+UseG1GC
  opennms.conf: OPENNMS_DATABASE_CONNECTION_MAXPOOL and MAXSIZE 250, MINPOOL 25
  opennms.conf: 13 daemons disabled (Pollerd, Bsmd, Ticketer, Correlator, Queued,
                Actiond, Notifd, Scriptd, Rtcd, SnmpPoller, EnhancedLinkd, Statsd,
                Ackd, PerspectivePoller); Syslogd enabled

  org.opennms.core.ipc.strategy kafka; org.opennms.timeseries.strategy osgi, no store
  provisiond, snmp-config and datacollection: no file on disk, compiled-in defaults

PostgreSQL, unchanged from the cleanroom run
  conf.d/10-benchmark-tuning.conf, pgtune web profile for 16 GiB / 8 vCPU
  max_connections 400, shared_buffers 3997MB, effective_cache_size 11993MB

figures.title: Collectd thread pool occupancy across the three fleet sizes
figures.note: JMX gauge from Collectd itself. Each rung is a 900 s window separated by a provisioning step; the pool fills as the fleet grows while CPU, below, barely moves.

figures.title: Collectd pending queue, rolling one-minute peak and floor
figures.note: The floor is the pass test. A floor that returns to zero every cycle is a fleet that completes; a floor that stays up is backlog.

figures.title: Collectd task completion ratio and collectable services
figures.note: The ratio is a sawtooth that resets at every cycle boundary; judge it on the median inside each rung. Services are divided by 1,000 to share the axis, so 2.0 is 2,004.

figures.title: Collections completed per second against the rate each fleet requires
Core CPU against the thread pool: the control
figures.note: Node Exporter for CPU, JMX for the pool, on one axis. Threads block on the SNMP round trip, so the pool fills while the processor stays idle. This is what thread-bound looks like.

figures.title: Core JVM heap and old-generation collections
figures.note: At these fleet sizes the JVM is not a factor; shown so the reader can see it was checked.

figures.title: Minion CPU and the SNMP bridge under injected latency
figures.note: The Minion executes the walks that the Core's threads wait on. Under latency it, too, is waiting rather than working.

answers.question: Where does Collectd stop completing its cycle at 50 to 100 ms per PDU?
What runs out, and what does not?
What does 50 to 100 ms of latency cost against the cleanroom?
How was the latency injected, and how was each rung measured?

gaps.question: Where exactly between rungs is the knee?
gaps.why: The step is 500 devices, so the knee is bracketed to within that, not located. Narrowing it means a rebuild at the last passing size with smaller steps.

gaps.question: Is uniform latency the right shape?
gaps.why: netem's default is uniform between the bounds. Real agent response time is heavy-tailed. Under Little's law the same mean should give the same pool occupancy, but that was not tested here.

gaps.question: Was each rung at steady state?
gaps.why: Each window opened after the rung's nodes reconciled to nodes x 144 interfaces and provisiond went idle, then a 300 s settle. One window per rung, three cycles, no repetition.

gaps.question: Do the simulated agents behave like real ones under latency?
gaps.why: netem delays every packet equally. A real agent that must query line cards delays the first PDU of a table walk more than the rest. The per-PDU cost is right; its distribution across a walk is not.
